requirement: Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST NOT offer a waiver for an uncited first-party Rust function. When a function serves only as an internal implementation detail and no existing requirement explains it, Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST direct agents to propose an explicit project requirement scoped to one area of internal code, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all requirement, obtain the user's agreement, mark the function with `{impl}`, and run `habeas author --all` for the harness to assess that requirement's evidence. That assessment MUST account for whether the requirement explains each implementing function's behavior. An internal-detail requirement MUST NOT justify an otherwise unspecified end-user-observable behavior.
rationale:
**Marking.** `requirements.cli.internal_detail_guidance` is anchored with `:impl:` to both bundled skills that carry its guidance, in `md/requirements/cli.md`. These are `assets/skills/habeas-requirements/SKILL.md` and `assets/skills/habeas-bootstrap-requirements/SKILL.md`. `md/reference.md` only cites the requirement. The requirement is about skill text, so it has no Rust implementation code.

**Obligations against the skill text:**
- **No waiver for an uncited function.** The requirements skill ("Reviewing code against requirements") says "there is no uncited-function waiver". The bootstrap skill says "There is no waiver for an uncited function."
- **Propose a scoped requirement, not a catch-all.** Both skills direct agents to propose an explicit requirement scoped to one area of internal code. Both use `internal.config_parsing` as the example and say "rather than one catch-all".
- **User agreement and `{impl}` marking.** Both skills say to "get the user's agreement" and to "mark the helper with `{impl}`".
- **Run `habeas author --all` so the harness assesses the evidence.**
  - The helper-specific paragraphs do not name the command.
  - The workflow sections do. In the requirements skill's "New or changed behavior" section, an agent runs it after implementing. In its "Authoring format" section, an agent runs it when a requirement changes. In the bootstrap skill, a dedicated paragraph runs it right after the helper paragraph.
  - The requirements skill also says "That requirement's review checks that it explains each implementing function."
  - This is somewhat implicit for the helper case, but it is adequately directed.
- **The assessment accounts for whether the requirement explains each implementing function.**
  - The requirements skill states this check outright.
  - It follows from the harness review criteria. The initial prompt in `md/requirements/authoring.md` makes behavior in `{impl}` code that the requirement does not specify a gap.
  - `md/reference.md` repeats the same point.
- **An internal-detail requirement MUST NOT justify unspecified user-visible behavior.** The requirements skill says "Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify otherwise unspecified observable behavior." The bootstrap skill says "Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify unspecified end-user-visible behavior."

**Tests.** No test checks the skill wording. The deliverable is prose guidance, so a test would only be string matching. The sibling guidance requirements (`behavior_review_guidance`, `requirements_review_skill`) have no such tests either. I judge their absence acceptable. Reading the skill sections against the requirement text is the practical verification.

**Extra behavior.** The skills contain much other guidance. Other requirements in `md/requirements/cli.md` anchor the same files and cover it: `info`, `bootstrap_skill`, `requirements_review_skill` and `behavior_review_guidance`. None of it is end-user-observable behavior beyond what the agreed requirements specify.

I found no unacknowledged gaps.
